idiom_name: nil placeholder; Object.new for stored slots, as_null_object for typed ones
implementation_notes: Ruby is duck-typed, so nil satisfies any positional parameter at runtime and needs no class, and Object.new is the placeholder for slots the system under test merely stores; optional parameters (def run(sink = nil)) often remove the need for a dummy altogether. RSpec's doubles are strict by default - any message that was neither allowed nor expected raises - so a plain double is a stub or spy, not a dummy; the dummy analogue is double('unused-sink').as_null_object, which returns itself for every message and allows arbitrarily deep chains. A suite that does not use rspec-mocks has the same two conventions available with no library at all: nil, and a plain Struct or Class.new instance with no behaviour.
code_sketch:
session = Session.new(config, nil, Object.new)   # clock and sink are never read here
session.run

# RSpec: a null-object double swallows messages instead of raising
sink = double('unused-sink').as_null_object
Session.new(config, nil, sink)
pitfalls: nil passes every parameter check but raises NoMethodError on the first call, so the diagnostic points into the SUT; if the interface might be touched, prefer a null-object double or a small empty class.
A plain RSpec double is strict by design: using one as a placeholder makes the test fail on the first unexpected message, which is a feature for stubs and a false alarm for an intended dummy.
as_null_object returns itself from every call, so a chain of calls never raises: a dummy that quietly satisfies code which should have failed can hide a path that now reads the parameter.
